title: How the Printing Press Changed the World
paragraphs: For centuries, the only way to reproduce a book was to copy it by hand, a task usually carried out by monks or trained scribes. Because a single manuscript could take months to complete, books remained scarce and costly, and owning one was largely a privilege of the Church, universities and the wealthy.

Around the middle of the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from Mainz, combined several existing technologies into a new system: movable metal type, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press adapted from those used to make wine. Individual letters could be arranged into pages, printed, and then reused.

The results were dramatic. Gutenberg’s Bible, completed around 1455, showed that printed books could be both beautiful and identical. By 1500, printers across Europe had produced millions of copies of thousands of different titles, and the price of books had fallen sharply.

Cheaper books encouraged literacy, while printed pamphlets allowed ideas to circulate faster than any authority could control them; the rapid spread of Martin Luther’s writings in the 1520s is a well-known example. Printing also helped scientists publish standardised texts and diagrams, laying the groundwork for modern scholarship.
